title: Straight-Line Motion: Position, Velocity, and Acceleration
subject: AP Calculus AB
objectives: Relate position, velocity, and acceleration as successive derivatives: v(t) = s'(t) and a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t).
Use the sign of velocity to determine direction of motion and find when a particle is at rest or changes direction.
Distinguish speed from velocity and determine when a particle is speeding up or slowing down.
Interpret position, velocity, and acceleration values in context with correct units.

sections.heading: Three Views of a Moving Particle
sections.content:
Picture a car driving along a straight road. At each moment you could record three different things: where it is (its position), how fast and which way it's going (its velocity), and whether it's pressing the gas or the brake (its acceleration). These three quantities are exactly the function s(t), its derivative, and its second derivative — and understanding how they fit together is one of the most heavily tested ideas on the AP exam.

Start with position s(t): the particle's signed location on a number line at time t. 'Signed' matters — positive means one direction from the origin, negative the other. Velocity v(t) = s'(t) is the rate at which position changes: how fast the particle moves and, through its sign, which direction. Acceleration a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t) is the rate at which velocity changes: it tells you whether the particle is gaining or losing velocity.

The key relationships are simply the derivative ladder you already know: differentiate position to get velocity, differentiate velocity to get acceleration. Everything in this lesson — finding when the particle is at rest, which way it's moving, whether it's speeding up — follows from reading the signs and zeros of these three functions. The mechanics are just differentiation; the challenge is interpretation.

sections.heading: Velocity, Speed, and Direction
sections.content:
Velocity and speed are not the same thing, and confusing them is a classic exam trap. Velocity v(t) is *signed*: its sign encodes direction. Speed is the *absolute value* of velocity, |v(t)| — it's how fast the particle moves regardless of direction, and it is never negative.

The sign of velocity tells you the direction of motion. If v(t) > 0, the particle moves in the positive direction (right, or up); if v(t) < 0, it moves in the negative direction (left, or down). When v(t) = 0, the particle is *instantaneously at rest* — and these moments are special, because they're the only times the particle can change direction.

To find when a particle changes direction, find where v(t) = 0 and check whether v actually switches sign there. A velocity that touches zero but keeps the same sign (like v = (t − 2)², which is zero at t = 2 but positive on both sides) means the particle paused momentarily without reversing. A velocity that crosses from positive to negative (or vice versa) at a zero means a genuine turnaround. This sign analysis — building a number line of v(t) — is the workhorse technique for the whole topic.

sections.heading: How to Analyze a Motion Problem

steps.title: Differentiate to get v and a
steps.content: From position s(t), compute velocity v(t) = s'(t) and acceleration a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t).

steps.title: Find the zeros of v (and a)
steps.content: Solve v(t) = 0 for the times the particle is at rest and possibly changes direction; solve a(t) = 0 for where acceleration changes sign.

steps.title: Build sign charts
steps.content: Mark the sign of v(t) on each interval (direction of motion) and the sign of a(t) on each interval, splitting at every zero of both.

steps.title: Read off the behavior
steps.content: Direction comes from the sign of v; the particle is at rest where v = 0 and changes direction where v changes sign; it speeds up where v and a share a sign and slows down where they differ.

sections.heading: Analyzing a Particle's Motion
sections.content:
A particle moves along a line with position s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t for t ≥ 0, where s is in meters and t in seconds.

Velocity: v(t) = s'(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t² − 4t + 3) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3).
Acceleration: a(t) = v'(t) = 6t − 12 = 6(t − 2).

When is the particle at rest? Set v(t) = 0: 3(t − 1)(t − 3) = 0, so t = 1 s and t = 3 s.

Which direction is it moving? Test the sign of v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) on each interval:
  On (0, 1): both factors negative → product positive → v > 0 → moving in the positive direction.
  On (1, 3): (t − 1) positive, (t − 3) negative → v < 0 → moving in the negative direction.
  On (3, ∞): both positive → v > 0 → moving in the positive direction.

So the particle changes direction at t = 1 (right to left) and again at t = 3 (left to right), because v changes sign at each.

Velocity at a moment: v(2) = 3(1)(−1) = −3 m/s, so at t = 2 the particle moves left at a speed of 3 m/s.
Acceleration there: a(2) = 6(2) − 12 = 0 m/s².

sections.heading: Speed Is |Velocity| — and 'Speeding Up' Has a Rule
sections.content: Two traps live here. First, speed is the absolute value of velocity; a particle with v = −5 has speed 5, and a more negative velocity (say −8) means a HIGHER speed even though the number is smaller. Second, a negative acceleration does NOT always mean slowing down. Whether a particle speeds up depends on whether v and a have the SAME sign (speeding up) or OPPOSITE signs (slowing down). A particle moving left (v < 0) with negative acceleration (a < 0) is actually speeding up, because it's getting more negative — a frequent point-loser on the exam.

sections.question: A particle has velocity v(2) = −4 m/s and acceleration a(2) = −3 m/s². At t = 2, the particle is:
sections.explanation: Velocity is negative, so the particle moves in the negative direction (left). Velocity and acceleration have the same sign (both negative), so speed is increasing — the particle is speeding up. Same signs always mean speeding up, regardless of whether they are positive or negative.

sections.heading: Speeding Up vs. Slowing Down
sections.content:
The rule worth burning into memory: a particle is *speeding up* when velocity and acceleration have the *same sign*, and *slowing down* when they have *opposite signs*. Speed (the magnitude |v|) increases exactly when the acceleration pushes in the same direction the particle is already moving, and decreases when acceleration opposes the motion.

Think about driving. If you're moving forward (v > 0) and press the gas (a > 0), you speed up — same signs. If you're moving forward (v > 0) and brake (a < 0), you slow down — opposite signs. Now reverse: if you're backing up (v < 0) and press the reverse pedal harder (a < 0), you back up faster — same signs, speeding up. If you're backing up (v < 0) but apply the brake (a > 0), you slow your backward motion — opposite signs, slowing down.

To analyze a whole motion, build sign charts for both v(t) and a(t) on the time line, then read off where their signs agree (speeding up) and disagree (slowing down). The transition points are the zeros of v (where direction may change) and the zeros of a (where acceleration changes sign, corresponding to inflection points of position).

sections.heading: Where Is the Particle Speeding Up?
sections.content:
Using the same particle, v(t) = 3(t − 1)(t − 3) and a(t) = 6(t − 2), determine when it is speeding up on 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.

Sign of v(t): positive on (0, 1), negative on (1, 3), positive on (3, 4).
Sign of a(t): a = 6(t − 2) is negative on (0, 2), positive on (2, 4).

Now compare signs on each subinterval split by the critical times t = 1, 2, 3:
  (0, 1): v > 0, a < 0 → opposite → slowing down.
  (1, 2): v < 0, a < 0 → same → speeding up.
  (2, 3): v < 0, a > 0 → opposite → slowing down.
  (3, 4): v > 0, a > 0 → same → speeding up.

So the particle is speeding up on (1, 2) and (3, 4), and slowing down on (0, 1) and (2, 3). Notice the analysis required splitting at every zero of both v and a — that's what creates the four subintervals.

sections.question: A particle moving along a line is at rest at exactly which times, given v(t) = (t − 2)(t − 5)?
sections.explanation: A particle is at rest when its velocity is zero. Setting v(t) = (t − 2)(t − 5) = 0 gives t = 2 and t = 5. These are also the candidate times for a change in direction, which would be confirmed by checking that v changes sign at each.

sections.heading: Exam Language and a Look Ahead to Distance
sections.content: On free response, 'find the velocity' means differentiate position once; 'find the acceleration' means differentiate twice; 'is the speed increasing?' means compare the signs of v and a at that instant. Always justify direction and speeding-up claims by citing the signs, not just the values. Coming in Unit 8: the integral of velocity over an interval gives displacement (net change in position), while the integral of speed |v(t)| gives total distance traveled — a distinction that builds directly on the velocity sign analysis you're practicing now.

sections.heading: Why Same Signs Mean Speeding Up
sections.content:
The rule 'same signs ⇒ speeding up' isn't a magic incantation — it falls out of calculus applied to speed itself. Speed is |v(t)|, and a particle speeds up exactly when |v(t)| is increasing, i.e. when the derivative of |v(t)| is positive.

Consider the two cases. When v > 0, speed equals v, so the rate of change of speed is just a; speed increases when a > 0 — same sign as v. When v < 0, speed equals −v, so the rate of change of speed is −a; speed increases when −a > 0, i.e. a < 0 — again the same sign as v. Either way, speed grows precisely when a shares v's sign.

There's an even slicker way to see it: the rate of change of speed is governed by the product v·a. When v·a > 0 (same signs), speed is increasing; when v·a < 0 (opposite signs), speed is decreasing. This is why some teachers tell you to 'just check the sign of v times a.'

The deeper point is that acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, but *speeding up* is about the rate of change of speed — and those differ by a sign exactly when the particle is moving in the negative direction. Keeping the distinction between velocity (signed) and speed (unsigned) straight is what makes every motion problem click into place.

For straight-line motion, v(t) = s'(t) and a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t). The sign of v gives direction (zero means at rest, a possible turnaround); speed is |v|. A particle speeds up when v and a share the same sign and slows down when their signs differ — equivalently, when the product v·a is positive or negative.

aiContext: AP Calculus AB Unit 4, straight-line (rectilinear) motion. Reinforce the derivative ladder s → v → a and that direction comes from the sign of velocity, with v = 0 marking possible direction changes that must be confirmed by a sign change. The make-or-break idea is that speed is |v|, so speeding up means v and a share a sign (equivalently v·a > 0), and a negative acceleration does not by itself mean slowing down — this is the most common error. Students should justify claims with sign charts of v and a rather than single values. Foreshadow Unit 8, where integrating velocity gives displacement and integrating speed gives total distance, both resting on this sign analysis.
